questions.question: Explain why the Moon shines at night, even though it does not make its own light.
questions.expected_answer: The Moon does not give out its own light. The Sun shines on the Moon, and the Moon's rocky surface reflects some of that sunlight to our eyes, just as a ball lights up when a torch shines on it. So moonlight is really reflected sunlight. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, and at full moon we see the whole lit half.

questions.question: What is a crater, how is it formed, and why do craters last so long on the Moon?
questions.expected_answer: A crater is a bowl-shaped hole with a raised rim. It forms when a rock from space, a meteoroid, smashes into the surface and blasts out rock and dust. Craters last for billions of years on the Moon because it has no air to burn up the rocks before they land, and no wind, rain or rivers to wear the craters away.

questions.question: Describe the mountains and plains on the Moon.
questions.expected_answer: Mountains are high, rough areas of rock, often in ranges or around the rims of big craters, and they make up the bright highlands. Plains are huge, flat, smooth, dark areas. They were once thought to be seas, but they are made of lava that flooded large basins and hardened long ago, and there is no water in them.
